story.fullStory:
Muddy Waters & The Rolling Stones's "Baby Please Don't Go" — original release 1981. "Baby, Please Don't Go" is a traditional  blues song that was popularized by Delta blues musician Big Joe Williams in 1935.

Many cover versions followed, leading to its description as "one of the most played, arranged, and rearranged pieces in blues history" by French music historian Gérard Herzhaft.

After World War II, Chicago blues and rhythm and blues artists adapted the song to newer music styles.

Muddy Waters (1913–1983) was an American blues artist who is considered a pioneer of the electric Chicago blues and a major influence on the development of blues and rock music.

approvedFacts.text: "Baby, Please Don't Go" is a traditional  blues song that was popularized by Delta blues musician Big Joe Williams in 1935.
Many cover versions followed, leading to its description as "one of the most played, arranged, and rearranged pieces in blues history" by French music historian Gérard Herzhaft.
After World War II, Chicago blues and rhythm and blues artists adapted the song to newer music styles.
Muddy Waters (1913–1983) was an American blues artist who is considered a pioneer of the electric Chicago blues and a major influence on the development of blues and rock music.

He popularized several early Delta blues songs, such as "Rollin' and Tumblin'", "Walkin' Blues", and "Baby, Please Don't Go", and recorded songs that went on to become blues standards, including "Hoochie Coochie Man",  "Mannish Boy", and "Got My Mojo Working".
